facts.title: A Symbol From Latin
facts.text: Lead's chemical symbol Pb comes from its Latin name plumbum, the same root that gives us the words plumber and plumbing because the Romans built their water pipes from it. Plumbum itself may trace back to an even older Mediterranean word for the metal. This is one of seven metals known since antiquity, alongside gold, silver, copper, iron, tin and mercury.

facts.title: Soft Enough To Scratch
facts.text: Lead is remarkably soft for a metal, with a Mohs hardness of only about 1.5, so you can scratch it with a fingernail and dent it with your thumb. It is also highly malleable and ductile, which let ancient craftsmen hammer it into sheets and pipes by hand. Despite this softness it is dense and heavy, which made it ideal for weights and seals.

facts.title: Surprisingly Heavy
facts.text: With a density of about 11.34 grams per cubic centimetre, lead is roughly 1.5 times denser than iron, so a small block feels startlingly heavy in the hand. This is why it has long been used for fishing sinkers, diving weights and the keels of sailboats. Its density also makes it an excellent absorber of X-rays and gamma rays.

facts.title: The End Of The Decay Line
facts.text: Lead is the final, stable resting place for three great radioactive decay chains: uranium-238 ends as lead-206, uranium-235 ends as lead-207, and thorium-232 ends as lead-208. Because of this, measuring the ratio of these lead isotopes in rocks is a cornerstone of uranium-lead dating, used to determine the age of the Earth. Lead-208 is also the heaviest completely stable atomic nucleus known.

facts.title: Shielding Against Radiation
facts.text: Its high density and many electrons make lead one of the best everyday materials for blocking ionizing radiation. That is why the heavy aprons worn during dental and medical X-rays contain lead, and why radioactive sources are stored in lead-lined containers called pigs. The same property protects technicians in nuclear facilities and hospitals.

facts.title: A Quiet Poison
facts.text: Lead has no known biological role and is toxic to humans, especially children, because it mimics calcium and disrupts the nervous system and the production of haemoglobin. Concern over this toxicity led many countries to phase out leaded gasoline, with the United States completing its road-fuel ban in 1996 and the very last nation, Algeria, ending sales in 2021. Old lead-based paint and plumbing remain important sources of exposure today.

facts.title: Sweet But Dangerous
facts.text: Lead compounds such as lead(II) acetate have a sweet taste, which earned the compound the historical nickname sugar of lead. The Romans boiled grape juice in lead pots to make a sweet syrup called sapa or defrutum used to preserve and sweeten wine. Historians debate how much this contributed to chronic lead poisoning among the Roman elite, but it shows how the metal's chemistry was exploited long before its dangers were understood.

facts.title: Powering Your Car
facts.text: The lead-acid battery, invented by French physicist Gaston Planté in 1859, was the first rechargeable battery and still starts the engine of almost every petrol and diesel car on the road. It uses lead and lead dioxide plates in sulfuric acid, and despite being old technology it is prized for delivering a large burst of current cheaply. Lead-acid batteries are also among the most recycled products in the world, with recovery rates above 95 percent in many countries.

facts.title: It Glides Under Pressure
facts.text: Lead exhibits creep, meaning it slowly flows and deforms under its own weight over years even at room temperature, which is why old lead roofing and church organ pipes can sag noticeably. It also becomes a superconductor when cooled below about 7.2 kelvin, conducting electricity with zero resistance. These two extremes show how differently the same metal behaves depending on temperature and time.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Most of the lead in the universe was created inside stars through the slow neutron-capture process, the s-process, in aging red giant stars, with additional amounts made in explosive events. Because so many radioactive isotopes ultimately decay into it, lead is more abundant in the cosmos than its high atomic number of 82 would otherwise suggest. On Earth it is mined mainly as the mineral galena, which is lead sulfide and often glitters with a metallic shine.
